abstract: ABSTRACT Background HER2‐positive breast cancer (BC), a highly aggressive malignancy, has been treated with the targeted therapy inetetamab for metastatic cases. Inetetamab (Cipterbin) is a recently approved targeted therapy for HER2‐positive metastatic BC, significantly prolonging patients' survival. Currently, there is no established biomarker to reliably predict or assess the therapeutic efficacy of inetetamab in BC patients. Methods This study harnesses the power of metabolomics and machine learning to uncover biomarkers for inetetamab in BC therapy. A total of 23 plasma samples from inetetamab‐treated BC patients were collected and stratified into responders and nonresponders. Ultra‐high‐performance liquid chromatography‐quadrupole time‐of‐flight mass spectrometry was utilized to analyze the metabolites in blood samples. A combination of univariate and multivariate statistical analyses was employed to identify these metabolites, and their biological functions were then ascertained by Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis. Finally, machine learning algorithms were employed to screen responsive biomarkers from all differentially expressed metabolites. Results Our finding revealed 6889 unique metabolites that were detected. Pathways like retinol metabolism, fatty acid biosynthesis, and steroid hormone biosynthesis were enriched for differentially expressed metabolites. Notably, two key metabolites associated with inetetamab response in BC were identified: FAPy‐adenine and 2‐Pyrocatechuic acid. There was some negative correlation between progress‐free survival (PFS) and their kurtosis content. Conclusions In summary, the identification of these two significant differential metabolites holds promise as potential biomarkers for evaluating and predicting inetetamab treatment outcomes in BC, ultimately contributing to the diagnosis of the disease and the discovery of prognostic markers.
methods:
2
Experimental
2.1
Inclusion Exclusion Criteria
This retrospective research study, conducted at Hunan Cancer Hospital from January to June 2023, enrolled 23 patients with advanced HER2‐positive breast cancer (
NCT05367739
). Ethical approval was granted by Ethics Committee and Institutional Review Board of the hospital (SBQLL‐2022‐066).
Inclusion criteria were as follows: Participants were aged between 26 and 72 years, with histologically confirmed advanced HER2+ disease and measurable disease in accordance with Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1 [
14
]. HER2 positivity was determined by a 3+ immunohistochemical score or by amplifying 2+ gene using fluorescence in situ hybridization. Positivity for the estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) was defined as ≥ 1% staining. Study participants' ER, PR, and HER2 expression levels were based upon the most recent tissue sample immunohistochemical results.
Trial endpoints: The primary endpoint was PFS, which was the time from first dose to first documented tumor progression or death from any cause. Secondary endpoint included objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR). The date of occurrence and severity of adverse reactions are based on the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Reactions (version 5.0). The groupings were as follows:
Responders (U‐A): Percentage of participants with complete response (CR) and partial response (PR) or percentage of participants with CR, PR, and stable disease (SD).
Nonresponders (N‐A): Percentage of participants with disease progression (PD).
Inetetamab (Cipterbin, 50 mg/bottle, Sunshine Guojian Pharmaceutical, Shanghai, China), the investigational drug, was administered initially at a dosage of 8 mg/kg and subsequently at 3 weeks' maintenance dose of 6 mg/kg, until the disease worsened or chemotherapy toxicity became intolerable.
2.2
Metabolites’ Extraction
A volume of 40 μL of plasma was added into 400 μL of methanol (preserved at −20°C), vortexed for 1 min, and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4°C. The entire supernatant was removed, placed in a new 2 mL centrifuge tube, concentrated, and dried. The residue was resolved by adding 150 μL of a solution of 2‐chloro‐l‐phenylalanine (4 ppm) made with 80% methanol water (kept at 4°C). Then, the supernatant was filtered using a 0.22 μm membrane and transferred to the detection vial for LC–MS detection.
2.3
Metabolites’ Detection
Conditions for liquid chromatography: Metabolite chromatographic separation was executed on a Vanquish UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The UHPLC system employed a T3 column (
C18150
× 2.1 mm, 1.8 μm) (Waters, Milford, MA, USA). Column temperature was set at 40°C. The flow rate and volume of injection were optimized at 0.25 mL/min and 2 μL. The LC‐ESI
+
‐MS analysis employed a mobile phase composed of a 0.1% formic acid aqueous solution (A) and a 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile mixture (B), with the gradient: 0–1 min, 2% C; 1–9 min, 2%–50% C; 9–12 min, 50%–98% C; 12–13.5 min, 98% C; 13.5–14 min, 98%–2% C; 14–20 min, 2% C. For the LC‐ESI
−
‐MS analysis, the gradient elution was as follows: 0–1 min, 2%A; 1–9 min, 2%–50%A; 9–12 min, 50%–98%A; 12–13.5 min, 98%A; 13.5–14 min, 98%–2%A; 14–17 min, 2%A.
Mass spectrometry conditions: Metabolites’ detection was performed by mass spectrometry using a Q‐Exactive HF‐X instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), fitted with an ESI ion source. Simultaneous MS and MS/MS (Full MS‐ddMS2 mode, data‐dependent MS/MS) acquisition was collected. Detected conditions were set as follows: Sheathed gas pressure at 30 arb, auxiliary gas flow at 10 arb, spray voltages of 3.50 kV for ESI
+
and − 2.50 kV for ESI
−
, capillary temperature at 325°C, an MS scan range of
m/z
81–1000 Da, MS resolving power of 60,000 FWHM, eight data‐dependent scans per cycle, MS/MS resolving power at 15,000 FWHM, normalized collision energy of 30%, and dynamic exclusion time set to automatic with a default duration.
2.4
Differential Metabolite Screening
LC‐MS‐based data processing: The acquired raw mass spectrometry (MS) data were initially transformed into the mzXML format by means of the MSConvert tool of the ProteoWizard software (version 3.0.8789). Subsequently, the XCMS package was employed for characteristic extraction, time for retention modification, and alignment. Metabolite identification was carried out on high accuracy mass (±20 ppm) and matching of MS/MS spectra to databases including Human Metabolome Database (HMDB,
http://www.hmdb.ca
), MassBank (
http://www.massbank.jp/
), mzCloud (
https://www.mzcloud.org
), and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG,
http://www.genome.jp/kegg/
).
Multivariate analysis screened differential metabolites: Metabolite matrix data were mean‐centered using scaling. Principal component analysis was initially utilized to discriminate metabolic phenotypes, and orthogonal partial least‐square discriminant analysis (OPLS‐DA) was used to discriminate differential metabolites. Permutation tests were used to check for excessive fitting in the OPLS‐DA model evaluation. Classes should not be predicted by the permuted model: R2 and Q2 values at the Y‐axis intercept must be less than those of Q2 and R2 of the nonpermuted model. OPLS‐DA enabled to screen for discriminative metabolites by means of the variable importance in projection (VIP). The P value, VIP generated by OPLS‐DA, and fold change were utilized to find the contributable variable for classification. Lastly, metabolites were considered statistically significant if the
p
value was less than 0.05, VIP values exceeded 1, and FC ratio > 2 or FC ratio < 0.5.
Pathway enrichment analysis related to differential metabolites: MetaboAnalyst, which integrated findings from robust pathway enrichment analysis with the pathway topology analysis, was used to analyze the pathways associated to differential metabolites. For biological interpretation of higher‐level systemic functions, the identified metabolites in metabolomics were then mapped to the KEGG pathway. The KEGG Mapper tool was utilized to visualize the metabolites and corresponding pathways.
2.5
Screen Biomarkers From Differential Metabolites Using Feature Engineering, Based on Explainable Machine Learning
Feature engineering for interpretable machine learning was employed to select candidate markers from differential metabolites. Differential metabolite datasets were divided into training and validation sets in a ratio of 7:3, and various machine learning models, such as random forests, support vector machines, and logistic regression, were built based on the training set, and the validation set was used to verify these models. Further, the accuracy, F‐measure, and AUC metrics are used to evaluate the models. Among them, the value of AUC ranges between (0, 1), and the closer the AUC is to 1, the better the model performance is. Further, the interpretability index SHAP value was utilized for feature selection, and TOP20 biomarkers were selected from the differential metabolites; the larger the SHAP value, the greater the metabolite's contribution to the classification and the more potential it is to become a candidate marker. Finally, random forest, support vector machine, and logistic regression algorithms were integrated to take the intersection to obtain the pharmacodynamic markers of inetetamab [
15
].

1
Introduction
Across the world, breast cancer has become the most frequent malignant tumor [
1
,
2
], with extremely high morbidity and mortality rates [
3
,
4
]. Although significant advances in early detection and treatment strategies have reduced the mortality rate of breast cancer, recurrence and metastasis are still the main causes of patients' death [
5
,
6
]. Compared with traditional chemotherapy, targeted monoclonal antibody drugs not only have higher efficacy but also can significantly improve the quality of life of patients.
Inetetamab, China's pioneering monoclonal antibody [
7
], focuses on the structural domain IV of the human epidermal growth factor‐2 (HER‐2) receptor to prevent the binding of epidermal growth factor, thereby inhibiting breast cancer cell proliferation. In contrast to trastuzumab, inetetamab possessed a unique amino acid sequence at the 359 and 361 sites of the heavy‐chain constant region of its Fc domain [
8
]. This distinct design enhances inetetamab‐dependent cell‐mediated cytotoxicity and reduces immunogenicity and adverse reactions [
9
], thereby granting it a central role in comprehensive anti‐HER2 therapy for breast cancer. Due to these unique pharmacological properties, inetetamab has become a fundamental drug for the whole anti‐HER2 treatment of breast cancer.
Currently, it is now well‐established that inetetamab specifically targets HER2 in breast cancer therapy; however, the underlying mechanism by which it modulates metabolic processes in this context remains elusive. With the continuous advancement of histology technology, a large amount of biological data has been accumulated, including genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics. Facing the challenges of high‐dimensionality and large data volume brought about by high‐throughput genomics data, machine learning algorithms have become a key tool for integrating and analyzing these complex data, thus contributing to the discovery of new biomarkers [
10
]. Yin et al. used a multi‐omics approach to whole exome sequencing (WES) and RNA sequencing of 233 samples from 50 breast cancer patients to identify and validate molecular signatures associated with response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. This study revealed the genomic and transcriptomic profiles of breast cancers before and after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and identified multi‐omics molecular signatures and potential biomarkers associated with responsiveness to and prognosis of neoadjuvant chemotherapy [
11
]. Jiang et al. conducted a multi‐omics analysis of 773 Chinese breast cancer patients to reveal the clinical and molecular characteristics of this population, including the tumor microenvironment, gene mutations, multi‐omics data, and their interrelationships, and used machine learning models for prediction and classification [
12
]. In addition, the investigators constructed and independently validated biomarkers of tumor microenvironment phenotypes for predicting immunotherapy response using a machine learning‐based radiomics approach [
13
]. This study aims to investigate metabolic biomarkers associated with the therapeutic efficacy of inetetamab in breast cancer from a biochemical standpoint. Through a comparative analysis of metabolic profiles in responders and nonresponders to inetetamab, the study employs advanced statistical techniques, including univariate analysis, multivariate analysis, and machine learning algorithms, to discern robust biomarkers indicative of its therapeutic impact on breast cancer. This research holds substantial promise for elucidating the mechanism of anti‐breast cancer treatment and forecasting the treatment outcomes of inetetamab.

3
Results
3.1
Medical Record Information
In this study, a total of 23 breast cancer patients (
n
= 9 for the control group and
n
= 14 for the inetetamab group) were enrolled from the Hunan Cancer Hospital. Plasma metabolomics detected a total of 6889 metabolites.
3.2
Univariate Analysis Screened Differential Metabolites
To discern metabolic biomarkers associated with inetetamab therapy, we compared metabolic differences using univariate analysis. A
t
‐test revealed 1837 metabolites with significant differences (
p
< 0.05) (Figure
1A
). Fold change analysis (FC) screened 2020 different metabolites, with 1881 upregulated and 139 downregulated following inetetamab treatment (Figure
1B
). Integrating the results from the
t
‐test and fold change analysis, 1602 metabolites with differential expression were screened (Figure
1C
).
FIGURE 1
Univariate statistical analysis screened differential metabolites. (A)
t
‐test: Red color dots represents
p
< 0.05; the difference is significantly different. (B) Fold change (FC): In order to filter the metabolites with more significant difference, the default selection is the substances with FC value ≥ 2 or ≤ 0.5. In order to present a better graphing effect, log
2
logarithm is usually taken for FC values in the analysis; if log
2
FC ≥ 1, it means this differential metabolite is upregulated, and if log
2
FC ≤ −1, it means this differential metabolite is downregulated. (C) Volcano plot of differential metabolites based on FC values and
p
values. Red dots represent differential metabolites that are significantly different and upregulated. Blue dots represent differential metabolites with significant differences and downregulation. Gray dots represent differences that are not statistically significant.
3.3
Multivariate Analysis Screened Differential Metabolites
Multivariate statistical analysis was performed to screen for differential metabolites. Principal component analysis (PCA) and hierarchical clustering distinguished metabolic phenotypes between patients receiving inetetamab therapy and those without it. Hierarchical clustering revealed a trend of separation between the inetetamab group and the control group, as well as sample clustering within each group, indicating that inetetamab treatment led to distinct metabolic phenotypes compared to no inetetamab treatment (Figure
2A
). Consistent with the hierarchical clustering results, PCA showed a separation tendency between the inetetamab group and the control group (Figure
2B
), suggesting that inetetamab therapy altered metabolic differences.
FIGURE 2
Metabolic phenotyping differentiated responders from nonresponders to inetetamab treatment in breast cancer patients. (A) Hierarchical cluster analysis. (B) Principal component analysis.
Classification analysis was performed using OPLS‐DA, which showed a significant separation of all plasma metabolites between the inetetamab therapy group and the control group (Figure
3A
). In order to check for overfitting in the OPLS‐DA model assessment, the permutation test was employed. A 200‐fold permutation test verified that the OPLS‐DA model was not overfit and exhibited high prediction accuracy (Figure
3B
). OPLS‐DA was capable of screening differentiated metabolites through the use of VIP values. By setting a VIP value higher than 1 as the screening criterion, 331 differential metabolites were identified in the S‐Plot of OPLS‐DA model, with 2‐Pyrocatechuic acid showing the most prominent decrease and 1‐deoxymethylsphinganine showing the most significant increase after inetetamab treatment (Figure
3C–E
).
FIGURE 3
Multivariate analysis screened differential metabolites. (A) OPLS‐DA model of N‐A patients and U‐A patients, which demonstrates the distribution of the inetetamab‐treated and control groups. (B) 200 permutation test. It proves model stability. (C) Metabolite scatter plot. The metabolites were deemed statistically significant if the
p
‐value was < 0.05, the VIP value was greater than 1, the FC ratio was greater than 2, or the FC ratio was less than 0.5. (D) Most significantly decreased differential metabolites. (E) Most significantly increased differential metabolites.
To further focus the key differential metabolites, we integrated univariate analysis with multivariate analysis to obtained 289 common‐differential metabolites (Figure
4
).
FIGURE 4
Integrated univariate statistical analysis and multivariate statistical methods to identify differentially expressed metabolites. Venn diagram of the intersection of
t
‐test, FC, and MVA significantly differential metabolites.
3.4
Enrichment Analysis
The 289 cross‐differentially expressed metabolites were screened through statistical variability. Comprehensive pathway analysis disclosed differentially expressed metabolites were predominantly involved in key metabolic processes such as retinol metabolism, fatty acid biosynthesis, steroid hormone biosynthesis, vitamin B6 metabolism, thiamine metabolism, CYP450‐mediated xenobiotic metabolism, pyrimidine metabolism, alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism, as well as butanoate metabolism. This finding suggested that inetetamab therapy exerted multifaceted metabolic modulation to effectively combat breast cancer (Figure
5
).
FIGURE 5
KEGG pathway analysis of 289 differentially expressed metabolites. (A) Bar scatter of KEGG pathway. (B) Bubble diagram of KEGG pathway. The bar scatter shows the enriched metabolites and pathways. For bubble diagram, the color of the dots reflects the enrichment
p
‐value, and the size reflects the enrichment ratio.
3.5
Machine Learning Screened Potential Markers
To further narrow down biomarker candidates, 289 metabolites were subjected to feature selection using three interpretable machine learning methods to identify important biomarkers. The differential metabolite dataset was split into training and validation sets with a 7:3 ratio at random. Machine learning models were built based on the training set, such as logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), and random forest (RF) models were employed for further biomarker screening, and these models were validated using the validation set. The metabolites were screened using logistic regression, support vector machine, and random forest, and then their intersection was used as an optimal biomarker.
The ROC curve is a tool for evaluating the performance of a binary classification model, which demonstrates the performance of the model at different thresholds by graphing the true and false‐positive rates. The area under the ROC curve is a measure of the performance of the model, and the higher the value of the AUC, the better the performance of the model. The logistic regression analysis revealed an AUC of 0.995 for the training set and 0.780 for the validation set, with a perfect recall rate of 1 and 0.869 for training set and validation set (Figure
6A–D
). The confusion matrix showed approximately 100% correct classification rate for the training set and 79.8% for the validation set. The model demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity. Furthermore, the interpretability index SHAP value was used for feature selection to select the TOP 20 biomarkers from the differential metabolites (Figure
6E–H
).
FIGURE 6
Logistic regression for selecting important metabolites from differential metabolites. (A) ROC curve for the training set. (B) ROC curve for the test set. (C) Recall curve for the training set. (D) Recall curve for the test set. (E) Confusion matrix for the training set. (F) Confusion matrix for the test set. (G) Top 20 differential metabolites ranked by SHAP. (H) Top 20 differential metabolites ranked by SHAP. The greater the SHAP value, the greater the contribution of the metabolite to classification.
Both SVM and RF models exhibited AUCs of 0.995 on both the training and validation sets, indicating high classification performance. The recall curves showed perfect AP values of 1.000, reinforcing the models' accuracy. The confusion matrices demonstrated that both models correctly classified about 100% of the differentiating metabolites in both sets. Selection of top 20 biomarkers of SHAP values from differential metabolites (Figures
7
and
8
).
FIGURE 7
Random forest for selecting important metabolites from differential metabolites. (A) ROC curve for the training set. (B) ROC curve for the test set. (C) Recall curve for the training set. (D) Recall curve for the test set. (E) Confusion matrix for the training set. (F) Confusion matrix for the test set. (G) Top 20 differential metabolites ranked by SHAP. (H) Top 20 differential metabolites ranked by SHAP. The greater the SHAP value, the greater the contribution of the metabolite to classification.
FIGURE 8
Support vector machine for selecting important metabolites from differential metabolites. (A) ROC curve for the training set. (B) ROC curve for the test set. (C) Recall curve for the training set. (D) Recall curve for the test set. (E) Confusion matrix for the training set. (F) Confusion matrix for the test set. (G) Top 20 differential metabolites ranked by SHAP. (H) Top 20 differential metabolites ranked by SHAP. The greater the SHAP value, the greater the contribution of the metabolite to classification.
By intersecting the metabolites from logistic regression, support vector machines, and random forest based on SHAP rankings, two feature metabolites were obtained: FAPy‐adenine and 2‐Pyrocatechuic acid (2,3‐dihydroxybenzoic acid) (Figure
9A
). After inetetamab was administered, there was a significant reduction in the levels of FAPy‐adenine and 2,3‐dihydroxybenzoic acid in the plasma (Figure
9B–9C
). The correlation of effective time of dosing PFS with the relative content of pharmacodynamic markers FAPy‐adenine and 2‐Pyrocatechuic acid was analyzed using Pearson methods, and the results showed that the effective time of dosing PFS had some negative correlation with the relative content of FAPy‐adenine and 2,3‐dihydroxybenzoic acid, with the Pearson correlation coefficient of −0.639728834 and −0.510989745, respectively (Table
S1
).
FIGURE 9
Integrated logistic regression, random forest, and support vector machines were employed to screen for significant metabolites as biomarkers. (A) Venn diagram of the intersection of Lasso, RF, and SVM significantly differential metabolites. (B‐C) Peak areas of FAPy‐adenine and 2,3‐dihydroxybenzoic acid in NA and UA groups respectively.
4
Discussion
The therapeutic response to monoclonal antibody immunotherapy is limited, and the adoption of efficacy markers is crucial for monitoring drug performance in oncology. Despite this, monoclonal antibody therapies often lack effective markers. Many antibodies exert their antitumor effects by addressing metabolic imbalances. In our study, we employed serum metabolomics to identify inetetamab's pharmacodynamic biomarkers. The rapid advancements in liquid mass spectrometry have led to a substantial accumulation of metabolite data, yet traditional statistical methods are inadequate for handling the large‐scale omics data. Machine learning demonstrates a broader scope and utility in analyzing and extracting valuable insights from extensive clinical histology data [
16
], particularly in discerning disease subtypes and biomarker discovery. We proposed a composite machine learning algorithm to efficiently process, analyze, and mine metabolomics data, thereby identifying two key metabolites, FAPy‐ adenine and 2,3‐dihydroxybenzoic acid, that significantly contributed to the response of inetetamab in breast cancer treatment.
Our finding highlighted the role of inetetamab in modulating multiple metabolic pathways contributing to its anti‐breast cancer efficacy, particularly focusing on “retinol metabolism,” “fatty acid biosynthesis,” and “steroid hormone biosynthesis.” Metabolic reprogramming plays an important role in cancer, where the metabolic patterns in tumor cells are significantly different from those of normal cells, the phenomenon of tumor cells reprogramming certain metabolic processes. Its characteristics include glycolysis, glutaminolysis, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, pentose phosphate pathway, and upregulation of other biosynthetic and bioenergy pathways [
17
,
18
]. Cancer metabolic reprogramming drives tumor formation by promoting and making possible rapid proliferation, survival, invasion, metastasis, and treatment resistance, among other key tumorigenic processes. On the other side, as tumors progress, cancer cells accumulate additional mutations and alterations that further intensify metabolic reprogramming, thereby accelerating tumor growth, proliferation, and progression [
17
]. The metabolism of cancer cells is heterogeneous and exerts different effects on the progression of different cancers. Some studies have shown that metabolic reprogramming is closely associated with malignant tumor growth, metastasis, invasion, and poor prognosis [
19
,
20
,
21
]. Tumor therapeutics targeting metabolic reprogramming have great research value and broad application prospects and can offer fresh insights and ideas for treating malignant tumors; thus, targeting metabolic reprogramming is a new direction for reversing immunosuppression. Monoclonal antibody drugs have a regulatory inhibitory effect on metabolic enzymes or related signaling pathways that may inhibit tumor progression.
Based on machine learning, we have ultimately identified FAPy‐adenine and 2,3‐dihydroxybenzoic acid as potential metabolites that mediate the response to inetetamab in breast cancer treatment. Adenine plays a role in regulating breast cancer cell death; depleting it can initiate apoptosis in triple‐negative breast cancer cells [
22
]. Notably, suppressing the antioxidant function of PRDX1/2 by adenine leads to a significant decrease in ERα levels in breast cancer cells. The study's limitation stems from the limited sample size of the experimental group, necessitating extensive validation of FAPy adenine and 2,3‐dihydroxybenzoic acid's diagnostic efficacy in breast cancer with larger cohorts. Future research should intensively investigate these compounds' biological roles in breast cancer treatment within the molecular biology context.
5
Conclusions
In summary, this study employed plasma metabolomics and machine learning techniques to identify differential metabolites between patients with breast cancer receiving inetetamab and those in the control group. Following metabolic pathway enrichment analysis of these differences, inetetamab therapy effected multiple various metabolic pathways in breast cancer. This underscores the significant utility of integrating metabolomics and machine learning methodologies in the diagnosis and treatment of breast cancer. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the mechanism by which inetetamab impacts breast cancer and offers insights for monitoring the treatment response of inetetamab.
